3426.prule: Word stress (diin) is a property of the individual word, marked in the orthography by an acute accent on the stressed syllable; it falls on the penult (words pronounced malumay: áhu, dúngu, lábuk, úu) or on the final syllable (words pronounced mabilis: buyá, buktút, maí, tuúk, mangán), and the diacritics are prescribed to distinguish words spelled alike but different in meaning, i.e. stress is contrastive. No default position, no counting rule, no weight condition is stated anywhere in the booklet; same-shape words take either position (áhu vs buyá, úu vs tuúk). Grave = penult stress plus final glottal stop (malumì: kakà, dirà, gawù); circumflex = final stress plus final glottal stop (kalupî, hirâ).

tn.quote: Ang mga suprasegmental ay hindi tulad ng segment na tumutukoy sa mga indibidwal na tunog. Ang mga ito ay tumutukoy sa kalidad ng mga tunog na makikita sa isang pantig, salita, o parirala. Ang mga suprasegmental na katangiang kadalasang matatagpuan sa isang wika ay ang haba (length), diin (stress), pitch (taas), intonasyon (intonation), at tono (tone). Dahil sa mga limitasyon sa pangangalap ng datos, tanging ang haba at diin lamang ang tinalakay sa bahaging ito.
tn.translation: Suprasegmentals are unlike segments, which refer to individual sounds. They refer to the quality of sounds found in a syllable, word, or phrase. The suprasegmental features usually found in a language are length, stress, pitch, intonation, and tone. Because of limitations in data gathering, only length and stress are discussed in this section.

3430.dloc: Ch. 2 'ਬੌਰੀਆ ਭਾਸ਼ਾ: ਧੁਨੀ-ਵਿਉਂਤ' [Bauria: phonology], section '(ੳ) ਬਲ਼ (Stress)' > 'ਬੌਰੀਆ ਭਾਸ਼ਾ ਵਿਚ ਬਲ਼', pp. 44-45. Restated ch. 4 pp. 141-142 and ch. 5 pp. 180-181. Tone: ch. 2 pp. 46-49.
3430.prule: Stress ('bal') in Bauria is sentence-level emphasis: according to the speaker's situation it is placed on some particular word of the sentence, and the stressed word is pronounced longer (rule 1, with question/assertion pairs chhio ahai jaegai? / chhio ahain jaegai); the word preceding the emphatic particle /tau/ (= Punjabi taan 'indeed') carries stress (rule 2: Harhman TAU jaegai 'Harman does go'). At the word level 'stress' is identified with what the Gurmukhi addak marks, i.e. consonant gemination (pato 'know' vs patto 'lesson', maghi 'simmer' vs magghi 'small pot', kad 'height' vs kadd 'when'). No rule for which syllable of a word is prominent is given anywhere in the thesis.
3430.srule: Not mentioned in Singh 2025 (ch. 2 '(ੳ) ਬਲ਼ (Stress)' pp. 44-45, introduced p. 43; restated ch. 4 pp. 141-142, ch. 5 pp. 180-181): the thesis treats 'stress' only as sentence-level emphasis and as word-level gemination (addak); no secondary or rhythmic stress is described.

tn.translation: In the Bauria language 'tone' is considered important. In Bauria communication all three forms of 'tone' are present. See examples: (1) tali - low tone: ta˄li (palm of the hand) ... mid tone: tali (spreading soil on the ground) ... high tone: ta˅li (to fry) ... The Bauria language abounds in words carrying two 'tones'. ... 'Tone' is found at word and at sentence level. All three forms of tone, low, mid and high, are met with.

Maggio 1749/1880, Gramática Cap. I 'Del Acento y Declinación', p. 1 (= PDF leaf 14; also quoted in Danielsen's fn. 88, p. 64). Admiraal 2016: 76.
3431.heavy: Heavy = syllables with the strong vowels /a/ ('Syllables that include the open back vowel /a/ are automatically heavy syllables and generally attract stress', p. 34) and /e/, 'heavy /i/' and the diphthong /oe/ ('which is also heavy', p. 65), and word-final glottalized vowels ('the final glottal stop makes the syllable heavy enough to be pronounced by itself', p. 64). Light = syllables with the weak vowels /o/ and weak /i/, 'which both cause a phonological process on the preceding phoneme so that the syllable phonetically gets lost' (p. 65). Phonetically closed suffix syllables attract secondary stress (p. 67). Vowel length is not phonemic (length accompanies stress).
3431.dflt: Second syllable of the phonological word; in a disyllable whose final syllable is light (weak /o/ or /i/), the first syllable.
3431.prule: Weight-sensitive, left-edge, stated with hedges. Primary stress falls 'quite regularly' on the second syllable of the underlying phonological word in three- and four-syllable noun roots (simóri, kaháp(o), asówa', erápoe'; epánoki, mokóvore) and, in verbs, 'on the second syllable if it is a syllable of the stem'. In disyllabic nouns the second syllable is stressed when it is heavy (vowels /a/, /e/, heavy /i/, diphthong /oe/, glottalized final: sipá', siyé', kohí') and stress retracts to the first syllable when the final syllable is light (weak /o/ or weak /i/, which elide or palatalize: hópi, ání, hím(o), tót(o)). A heavy /a/ syllable attracts stress away from the second syllable (etonánev 'women' vs. éton). Stress is not contrastive; the stressed syllable is louder, longer and high-pitched. Danielsen cites Magio's 1749 penultimate claim (fn. 88) and sets it aside in favour of Baptista & Wallin's second-syllable generalization.
3431.srule: Words of up to four syllables generally have one stress. In words longer than four syllables there is a secondary stress, never on a syllable adjacent to the primary; grammatical suffixes can carry it, generally when they contain a strong vowel /a/ or /e/ or are pronounced as closed syllables. Example: nasórohèyow [naˈsɔroˌhejow] na.so.ro.he.yow (. x. x.) 'where I am very strong' (ex. 139) vs. four-syllable nasórohew with one stress peak (ex. 140).

3431.cfw: Danielsen (2007), the only modern phonological description, puts Baure stress on the second syllable from the left with vowel weight deciding disyllables and endorses Baptista and Wallin's (1968) second-syllable finding; the sole dissent, Maggio's 1749 missionary grammar with its "usually penultimate, often antepenultimate, sometimes final", is older, gives no conditioning and largely matches that same pattern counted from the right, so the reading is clear but rests on few sources and on Danielsen's own hedges.

For the purpose of stress placement an off-glide functions as a closed syllable when it occurs in word final position.

3432.heavy: A ‘closed syllable’ (CVC, in any position: [du.ˈɑn] final, [ɑ.ˈgin.Ɂɑi] medial, [ˈlɛs.ɑ.lɛs] initial); additionally ‘an off-glide functions as a closed syllable when it occurs in word final position’, i.e. a word-final vowel+off-glide syllable ([ɑu], [ɑi], [ɛi]: [fu.ˈɑu] ‘red ant’, [hɑ.Ɂi.ˈsɑi] ‘where?’, [su.lɑ.ˈpɑi] ‘star’ p. 3, [bi.ˈɑi] ‘aunt’ p. 5, [u.ˈfɛi] ‘wind’ p. 6). The source lists /ɛi ɑi oi ou ɑu/ under ‘Vowels’ (p. 4) and its syllable-pattern table (p. 9) has VV, CVV and CVVC types ([ɑu], [lɑi], [dɑul]), so the off-glide is part of a diphthongal nucleus and a word-final (C)VV syllable is heavy for stress; non-final (C)VV is not said to count as heavy.

3432.prule: Monomorphemic words: stress on the first (leftmost) closed syllable, wherever it falls (final [du.ˈɑn], medial [ɑ.ˈgin.Ɂɑi], initial [ˈlɛs.ɑ.lɛs]); a word-final off-glide (V+glide, e.g. [fu.ˈɑu], [hɑ.Ɂi.ˈsɑi]) counts as a closed syllable; if the word has no closed syllable, stress the first syllable ([ˈgɑ.gɑ.tu], [ˈsɑ.gi.gi.li]). Polymorphemic words are grammatically conditioned: inalienably possessed nouns take main stress on the final syllable; verbs stress the subject-agreement suffix, aspect/mood/negative marker, infinitive clitic or object marker depending on the conjugation.

tn.quote: La langue beembe comporte deux tons ponctuels: l'un normal (ou bas), l'autre haut. Le ton est supporté par le noyau syllabique qui peut être une voyelle brève, une voyelle longue, ou deux voyelles en contact. L'unité prosodique est égale à une more, analogue par la durée à une voyelle brève: deux tons consécutifs dans la même syllabe peuvent être de même registre, c'est-à-dire tous deux bas ou tous deux hauts, ou bien présenter un contraste bas-haut ou haut-bas. Le ton a une fonction distinctive, et par exemple /tù-súːb-à/ 'nous achèterons' est distingué de /tù-sùːb-à/ 'nous achetons'.
tn.translation: Beembe has two punctual tones: one normal (or low), the other high. Tone is carried by the syllable nucleus, which may be a short vowel, a long vowel, or two vowels in contact. The prosodic unit equals one mora, analogous in duration to a short vowel: two consecutive tones in the same syllable may be of the same register, i.e. both low or both high, or show a low-high or high-low contrast. Tone has a distinctive function, e.g. /tù-súːb-à/ 'we will buy' is distinguished from /tù-sùːb-à/ 'we buy'.

3439.prule: Accent on the initial syllable of the nominal or verbal stem (thème): the stem-initial syllable is labelled strong (s) and the adjacent stem syllable(s) weak (w), building trochees; noun-class prefixes and connectives lie outside the accent domain, so the position is fixed relative to the stem, not the word ('accent libre' = morphologically conditioned, vs. 'accent fixe' as in French); quantity-insensitive (the mora plays no role).
3439.srule: No secondary or rhythmic accent within the simple word: one left-headed, maximally binary foot is built per phonological word (= noun/verb stem), so each stem carries a single, stem-initial prominence (Bouka 1995: 211, [86]); in lexicalised compounds (N + connective + N) each nominal stem is its own prominence domain, i.e. one accent per stem (p. 340). Bouka does not use the term 'accent secondaire' for Bekwel.
3439.quote: L’unité accentuelle, en bekwel, est le mot phonologique. Ce dernier correspond soit à une base nominale, soit à une base verbale. 3439.tone: Bekwel is at the same time a tone language: three basic tonetic levels (haut H, bas B, haut abaissé) plus contour tones BH and HB, which occur on short as well as long vowels (§5.22.1, p. 341); tonemes H and B. Bouka argues the accent is not reducible to pitch ('cette langue offre un cas-type où les manifestations de l’accent ne se laissent pas réduire au fonctionnement de la hauteur mélodique', p. 334), citing vowel length, a/0 alternation, resistance to semi-vowel reduction, tonal stability of the accented syllable and its attraction of contour tones (pp. 334-337); but he states that the phonetic nature of the accent could not be investigated further (p. 331) and concludes that a diacritic accent is necessary to account for the tonal processes (p. 372).
